chapter_theme: Poems 341 to 355 are magatpaal kaanchi: a chieftain refuses his daughter to kings, and the poet sees the town's groves, fords and walls about to be ruined by the war her beauty brings. Poems 356 to 360 are perunkaanchi: the burning ground outlives all rulers, so kings are told to give while they can.

341.reading: A chieftain refuses his young daughter even to a king who pleads, calls his fierce kin to the flower-taking of war and wades into the pond, torn between wedding her tomorrow and entering the world of no return with a spear-scarred body; the poet fears the cool field-town will lose its beauty like a pool churned by fighting elephants.
341.nuance: The hero (குருசில்) is given the choice as a pair of 'one or the other' (ஒன்றோ ... ஒன்று): the wedding day and the warrior's death are set as equal outcomes, and the poet's own worry is for the town, not for either man.

thinai_evidence.note: a refused bride brings war, and the poem weighs death against the town's ruin

comparisons.tenor: the field-town about to be spoiled

342.reading: Asked by an eager spear-bearing lord whose daughter the broad-shouldered girl with the dark flower garland is, the speaker answers that her beauty is for warriors alone: her father owns rich fields where heron chicks feed on fish eggs and prawn, and because kings could not win her, her brothers thresh the battlefield daily with swords, using heaped corpses as sheaves and broken elephants as oxen.
342.nuance: The heron chick that eats its fill and still finds eggs and prawn is a picture of the father's plenty; it is set against the brothers' harvest of corpses, so the poem's two 'fields' are the paddy land and the battlefield.

thinai_evidence.note: a girl withheld from kings and the war it causes

comparisons.tenor: the battlefield as a threshing floor, its corpses as sheaves and dying elephants as oxen

343.reading: Musiri, where fish is bartered for paddy, pepper sacks crowd the houses and the gold brought by ships comes ashore by canoe, belongs to Kuttuvan who gives the goods of hill and sea to comers; even if wealth like Musiri is humbly offered, the father says she will not be married to those not his equal, and the poet asks whether the walled town, with the attackers' ladders against it and kites resting on the inner wall, will not suffer.
343.nuance: The bride-price is measured by a real port's trade, gold coming in and pepper going out; the father's refusal is framed as rank (புரையர்), not price, so no wealth can settle it.

thinai_evidence.note: bride-price refused and a siege ladder already raised

comparisons.tenor: the great wealth offered as bride-price
Musiri's roaring sea as its drum

344.reading: The suitor will do one of two things, give a town of fields, where peacocks that ate red paddy fly up with the bangled women and settle on the marutham tree by the ford, together with great wealth, or spread smoky fire and enmity with graceless manliness; one of them is sure to come, because of the girl with the kaanchi-shoot garland and the lines on her waist.
344.nuance: The peacocks and the women rise together and settle in the marutham tree; whether the poet means them as one picture of the town's ease or likens the women to the birds is not fixed by the text.

thinai_evidence.note: the suitor's two courses, gift or war

345.reading: The groves are shaken by tethered elephants, the streets thick with chariot dust, the roads jammed with horses, the ford muddied by the washing of weapons, the ground bowed by the weight of fierce warriors: many new kings have come for the girl, and her lovers are to be pitied, for her brothers want war, not wealth, saying there is no giving to those out of line, and with shields, notched swords and blood-matted heads they are such men that the poet cries, what will become of this good town fenced with cotton?
345.nuance: The siege is told entirely through what it does to the town (grove, street, road, ford, ground) before the girl is named; lines 8 and 9 (the iron like a she-elephant's breath, the back like a painting) are obscure.

thinai_evidence.note: kings encamped around a town over a refused daughter

comparisons.tenor: the iron (bellows or goad) the hand grips

346.reading: The mother does not refuse her and the young man, strong and good with the bright spear, insists; if that comes true, the fallen will fall, the kin who remain will die with none to care for them, and the girl's beauty will make a great wasteland.
346.nuance: The last line makes the girl's beauty (நலன்) the grammatical agent of the ruin, the same move as 349's anangu.

thinai_evidence.note: a girl's beauty foreseen as the town's ruin

347.reading: Akuthai of fierce war, who drinks fragrant toddy, wears battle-withered thumbai and carries a spear notched in fight, holds a Koodal ringed by deep water, and the girl with heavy hair is likened to it; though the trees of our town are thick-trunked, they have shaken at the root since the kings tethered their trained elephants to them.
347.nuance: Line 8 is lost, so what the simile of Akuthai's Koodal is joined to cannot be read with certainty; the closing image of trees shaken at the root by tethered elephants recurs in 348.

thinai_evidence.note: kings' war elephants tethered in the girl's town

348.reading: The girl with kuvalai eyes is like Unur of truthful Thazhumban, where the drum of the rice reapers scares bees from the honey, toddy is strained in pots and the panar quarter scales fish; had her mother not borne her, the trees of our great ford would not suffer from long chariots standing in every shade and red-browed elephants tied at every place.
348.nuance: The counterfactual (had her mother not borne her) blames no one; the harm is told only through the trees, which is how the speaker can grieve without accusing the girl.

thinai_evidence.note: kings' chariots and elephants camped at the town for a girl

349.reading: The king wipes the sweat from his brow with his spear-point and speaks harsh words, and the father too speaks only proud words and never bows; that is their vow, so the girl with fine teeth and cool streaked eyes has become, like a small fire born in wood, a danger to the town she was born in.
349.nuance: The fire that is born in wood and burns the wood names exactly the girl's relation to her town; the poet calls her அணங்கு, a harmful power, not because of anything she does but because of two men's vows (படிவம்).

thinai_evidence.note: king and father both unbending over a daughter

comparisons.tenor: the girl who brings ruin on her own birthplace

350.reading: The old town with its moat filled in, its battlements sagging and its wall broken cannot hold out; kings with drums like falling thunder and fast horses come at dawn and circle our tall gate and will not leave without a fight, all for the freckles budding on the breast of the young girl whose eyes are red like her brothers' spears.
350.nuance: The poem ends on the smallest thing in it, the freckles on a young girl's breast, as the cause of a siege; her eyes are said to be red like her brothers' spears, which ties her beauty to the men who will fight for it.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem is about a besieged town's failing walls and gate

351.reading: Kings whose army is as wide as the sea, with belled elephants, flag-topped chariots, horses and warriors, will never rest without taking the girl whose beauty is like the vaakai of generous Eyinan; what will become of this secure field-town where the red-striped heron, tired of the honeyed marutham's branch, sleeps in the lovely kaanchi?
351.nuance: Whether வாகை here is Eyinan's victory or a place called Vaakai is not settled by the line. The heron that leaves the marutham for the kaanchi tree to sleep is a picture of the town's safety (ஏமம்), set against the army that threatens it.

thinai_evidence.note: a refused girl and the town's fate

352.reading: Through broken lines the poem sets milking, mullai picking with leaf cups and women with aambal-stalk bangles leaping into water beside a comparison with Uranthai of the great giver Thithan, ringed with white paddy; fine jewels like that town are offered and refused, and the girl's freckles shine like young vengai flowers.
352.nuance: So many lines are lost that who refuses the jewels and what the brothers do cannot be read.

thinai_evidence.note: bride-gifts offered and refused

353.reading: To the victorious lord who stopped his chariot, eyes pale, gazing at the girl in a gold-coin girdle and eekai garland, and keeps asking whose daughter she is, the speaker answers: she is the daughter of an old-line chieftain who never fails to feed the bowmen from grain heaps like hills, and her brothers, who answered the old kings who asked before with blood and still wear unchanged wound dressings, are men to fear.
353.nuance: The answer moves from the father's open-handed feeding of fighters to the brothers' wounds, so the girl's lineage is described as both generous and dangerous; line 13 is lost.

thinai_evidence.note: a king's question about a girl answered with her brothers' war record

354.reading: Spears that would not be stilled even if a king came against them are plunged in water, and the father turns back even worthy suitors; will the town, where the vaalai fish chased by the heron leaps from the field pond into the houses of bathing women, lose its beauty over the young girl's gaze, gentle as a doe's?
354.nuance: Lines 2 and 3 (spears plunged in water; the father 'turning back' even the worthy) admit more than one construction.

thinai_evidence.note: suitors turned back and the town's beauty at stake

355.reading: The fort has no battlements, its moat is so dry that calves graze and frisk in it; that is the state of the town; the rest is lost.
355.nuance: The calves playing in the dry moat make the town's helplessness almost comic; the colophon gives only the thinai and no thurai, poet or patron.

thinai_evidence.note: a fort's broken defences

356.reading: The old misty burning ground, with its salt waste, spreading cactus, owls hooting by day, pyre lamps and ghoul-women with crooked teeth, is fearful; the tears of loving kin quench the white ash of its bone-strewn pyres, and having seen the backs of everyone and become the end for all mankind, it has never seen the back of anyone who would see its back.
356.nuance: 'Seeing someone's back' is to outlast them (they turn and go); the ground has seen everyone's, and no one has seen its own, so the cremation ground, not any king, is the true survivor.

thinai_evidence.note: the burning ground outlasts everyone

357.reading: Even those who ruled without sharing the hill-bound earth that is common to three kings have seen their years end, and wealth was not what stayed as their support; when death takes life as kin weep, it is hard for those who let go of the raft to climb from this bank to the far one.
357.nuance: Line 6 is mostly lost, so what the raft (புணை) is, merit or giving, is inferred from the contrast with wealth in line 5.

thinai_evidence.note: death and what outlasts kingship

comparisons.tenor: the merit that carries one through death

358.reading: This rich earth circled by the sun has had seven owners in a single day; weighed against austerity the world is not worth a mustard seed of it, so those who loved it let it go; therefore Fortune does not leave those who leave her, and those who will not leave are left by her.
358.nuance: The last two lines turn on one verb (விடு) four times, so that leaving and being left are the same act seen from Fortune's side; the poem praises renunciation in a book of kings.

thinai_evidence.note: the impermanence of rule weighed against austerity

359.reading: The burning ground of hooting owls, corpse-eating jackals with fat-shining teeth and ghoul-women who clasp the dead, eat pale flesh and dance on the salt waste by the pyre lamps, has received even conquerors of kingdoms, and your day too will come; blame stays and fame stays, so put away blame, seek fame, speak good without wanting, and give elephants, gold-trapped horses and tall chariots freely to suppliants, and your fame will shine here long after you go.
359.nuance: 'Blame stays and fame stays' (line 10) makes the counsel a choice between two lasting names, not between a name and oblivion.

thinai_evidence.note: counsel to give drawn from the burning ground

360.reading: Few have ruled this land as a shelter for others, men slow to anger, of few words and much learning, of fine understanding and great giving, who served cool liquor and rich food and helped many; even their wealth does not abide, so keep your conduct faultless and fill the hands of gift-seekers, for after the pulaiyan sets out the rice offering on grass in the vulture-haunted cremation ground and the body enters the fire, those who shared their food will not remain.
360.nuance: The last line (பலர்வாய்த்து இராஅர்) can be read as 'they do not stay' or as a claim about being in many mouths; the sense of the close, whether sharers are remembered or simply die like all, is not settled. Line 10 carries a stray closing quotation mark.

thinai_evidence.note: counsel on the impermanence of wealth

links.note: Both close on the town's trees straining at the root because kings have tethered war elephants to them.
links.teaches: Kapilar and Paranar both show the coming war through the trees the kings' elephants are tied to, so this was a stock way of picturing harm to the town without blaming the girl.

links.note: 356 describes the burning ground as the survivor of all; 359 opens with the same ground and turns it into counsel to give.
links.teaches: The cremation-ground description that stands alone in 356 is the first half of an argument in 359, which shows it was a stock opening for perunkaanchi counsel to kings.

links.note: Both describe Musiri's trade: gold arriving by ship and pepper going out.
links.teaches: The same port appears from both sides of the genre line, and in both the speaker refuses Musiri-scale wealth for a woman: the father will not sell her, the hero will not leave her for it.

links.note: Both name Thazhumban and his town Unur.
links.teaches: The puram poem praises Thazhumban for truthful speech and the akam poem for never turning comers away, so his fame reached akam poets as that of a host and landmark, and both use his rich Unur as a byword for plenty.

links.note: Both name Eyinan; 351 likens the girl's beauty to his vaakai, while Akananuru 208 recalls his death at Paazhi. Uncertain: வாகை may be a victory or a place.
links.teaches: The puram poet uses Eyinan's vaakai as a measure of beauty while the akam poet uses his fall in battle as a measure of shame avenged, so one chieftain's name served both as a token of victory and of a hero's death.

links.note: The Kural calls it the world's 'greatness' that one here yesterday is gone today; 356 gives that greatness a place, the burning ground that has seen everyone's back.
links.teaches: The Kural's bitter abstraction becomes a physical place in the Purananuru, and the ground that outlives all men is the 'greatness' the couplet names without showing.

links.note: Both use crossing water as the image of what one needs at death; the Kural's swimmer needs the Lord's feet, 357's needs a raft that wealth is not.
links.teaches: The crossing image the Kural gives a god already stood in the Purananuru without one, carried by what a man keeps in place of wealth, so the Kural's theology was laid on an older ethical figure.

links.note: Both turn on one verb of holding or leaving repeated across the lines; the Kural says griefs cling to clingers, 358 that Fortune leaves those who cling and stays with those who let go.
links.teaches: Read together they give both halves of one argument the Kural states only negatively: holding brings grief, and letting go is what keeps Fortune, so renunciation is offered even to kings as a gain.

links.note: The Kural says nothing but renown stands undying; 359 says blame stands too.
links.teaches: Adding that blame lasts as well turns the Kural's consolation into a warning, so giving is urged not to earn a name but to escape the other lasting name.

links.note: Both say give now because death is certain; the Naladiyar warns that wealth is useless after the funeral drum, 359 promises a fame that outshines the burning ground.
links.teaches: The same deathbed counsel serves two motives: the Naladiyar argues from the uselessness of hoarded wealth, the Purananuru from the name left behind, so the later book drops the reward the earlier one offered.

links.note: The Kural says wealth does not stay, so do at once what stays; 360 says even great rulers' wealth does not stay, so fill the hands of gift-seekers.
links.teaches: The Kural leaves 'what stays' unnamed, and the Purananuru names it as filling the hands of those who seek gifts, which shows the bard's claim behind the maxim.

new_concepts.gloss: marriage, the formal taking of a bride; here the bride sought by kings and refused
the gift a patron gives to a bard or suppliant

source_issues: Purananuru 341 line 5 (அனரமண் இஞ்சி) looks corrupt, and line 6 is lost.
Purananuru 344 line 8 has a gap and line 9 (கணிமே வந்தவள்) is obscure.
Purananuru 346 line 1 and 347 line 8 are lost (347 line 9 is partial).
Purananuru 345 line 19 and 347 line 9 are the same formula (என்னா வதுகொல் தானே), flagged as a repeated line; it is a refrain of the magatpaal poems, not a copying error.
Purananuru 352 has gaps in lines 2, 8, 11, 12, 15 and 16, and 353 line 13 is lost.
Purananuru 355 has only four lines and no thurai, poet or patron in the colophon; Duraisamy Pillai's edition has two more lines before the gap.
Purananuru 357 line 6 is mostly lost and read differently by the two sources.
Purananuru 358's colophon thurai (மனையறம், துறவறம்) is not a thurai of the kaanchi list; the poem's content is renunciation only.
Purananuru 360 line 10 has a closing quotation mark with no opening one.
